title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization
authors: Zhuo Wang, Ce Yu, Bin Yang
abstract: Compact quantum neural networks have been explored for cloud-cover parameterization, but their predictive value depends on how physical knowledge is incorporated and which classical models provide the reference. We investigate an offline residual formulation that retains a fitted \XR\ cloud-cover estimate and learns a correction to its logit in transformed target space. Using released ICON/DYAMOND-derived data, we compare ten model variants in six- and eight-input settings, with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples per replicate. All quantum circuits use local Z readout and noiseless exact expectation values. Under a common 30-epoch protocol, residual prediction reduced physical-space test mean squared error relative to direct QNN prediction by 54.3\% and 38.8\% for six-input XYZ and ZZXY circuits, and by 49.2\% and 38.9\% for their eight-input versions. Residual QNNs also outperformed the selected compact residual multilayer perceptron in every paired replicate. A larger, longer-trained Grundner-Q1 adaptation nevertheless achieved lower error: residual Q1 reached mean MSEs of 0.00778 and 0.00791, compared with 0.01124 and 0.01082 for residual XYZ. The results support residual prediction for compact simulated QNNs within the tested budget and establish a clear boundary set by stronger classical references. They do not establish computational quantum advantage or online climate-model skill.
summary: This work proposes using residual quantum neural networks to improve cloud-cover parameterization in climate models. By training the QNN to predict only a correction term relative to an established physical estimate, the authors achieved substantial reductions in prediction error compared to direct methods. This demonstrates the power of physics-informed machine learning approaches within the quantum circuit framework.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of accurately parameterizing cloud cover in climate models, a process complicated by coarse spatial resolution and unresolved sub-grid physics.
main_result: Implementing a residual quantum neural network (QNN) formulation, which learns a correction to a known physical estimate, significantly reduced the test Mean Squared Error (MSE) compared to direct QNN prediction.
method: The authors employed an offline residual formulation, training a QNN to predict a correction term to the logit of a fitted Xu–Randall cloud-cover estimate, rather than predicting the cloud cover directly.
model_or_system: The physical system is cloud-cover parameterization within climate models, using data derived from ICON/DYAMOND simulations. The model utilizes compact QNNs with XYZ or ZZXY circuits as the parameterized function class.
key_observables: Physical-space test Mean Squared Error (MSE) for cloud fraction, $R^2$, Hellinger distance, and Wasserstein distance.
important_parameters: Training epochs (e.g., 30 epochs), number of inputs (six or eight), and the specific quantum circuit structure (XYZ, ZZXY).
main_assumptions: The results do not establish computational quantum advantage or online climate-model skill; the comparison is limited by the specific training budget and matched replicates.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the residual QNN structure, comparing test MSE reduction percentages between direct and residual predictions across different input configurations (6 vs 8 inputs).
paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical problem, details the residual QNN methodology (anchoring to Xu-Randall), presents quantitative comparisons against MLPs and Q1 models using various metrics, and concludes by discussing the limitations regarding quantum advantage.
why_interesting: While the application is climate science, the core methodology—using quantum circuits to learn corrections to physically constrained models—is highly relevant to developing physics-informed neural networks for complex quantum or many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Physics-anchored residual QNN. The fixed branch supplies logit a(x). The quantum branch supplies local expectations mi = ⟨Zi⟩to one affine head. Its zero initialization recovers the clipped anchor. The branches combine before the sigmoid, and the inverse target transform returns physical cloud cover. Training loss is evaluated before that inverse transform; the dashed arrow updates only trainable parameters. Overlapping blocks and representative wires abbreviate the six- or eight-qubit circuit, not its actual layer count. The figure’s T and Tx denote the target and input transforms.

Figure 2: Test-set performance across input configurations. Each row groups six-input (open) and eight- input (filled) bars, whose lengths show mean physical-space MSE. Small points represent three matched replicates; whiskers show ± one sample SD (n = 3, 20,000 test cells per replicate). QNNs are blue, Q1 adaptations ochre, and remaining controls gray. Every residual model is anchored to Xu–Randall; all QNNs use local Z readout. Q1 uses a larger architecture and a separate, longer training protocol. Axis values are expressed in units of 10−2; lower values indicate lower error. Source data: runs.csv and summary.csv.
